Replacing worn turf in Celebration's original villages and newer sections

Replacing worn-out turf in Celebration gets priced from what the tear-out finds, not a flat square-foot rate, since the base underneath and, on an older lawn, what infill comes out of it both weigh on labor more than area alone. The town's original villages go back to 1996, so a meaningful share of that turf now predates the state's infill rule and is old enough that replacement, not another repair, is the honest call.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Pre-2026 lawns sometimes carry an infill the state no longer allows

A lawn converted in one of Celebration's original villages before Rule 62-308.100 took effect on May 19, 2026 may have gone in with a rubber crumb infill, an ordinary choice at the time and now allowed only within the footprint of playground equipment. A full replacement is the point to correct that: pulling the old turf out takes the infill with it, and the new lawn goes back down with silica sand, zeolite or a coated sand product instead, while the base underneath gets rebuilt to the state's current washed, open-graded standard at the same time.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Celebration lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

Re-checking the pond setback on an older golf-lot or waterfront replacement

An older turf install on a Manor or Estate lot backing a pond or the golf course can predate the state's current 10-foot waterbody setback, and a full replacement is the point to bring the layout in line with that distance instead of relaying the same footprint that was there before. A seawall or bulkhead already standing between the yard and the water is the one case where that distance doesn't move the new edge.

Upgrading backing on a replacement instead of matching it

Backing technology has improved since many older Celebration lawns went in, and a replacement is a natural point to move up from a semi-perforated or lower-rated backing to a fully permeable product rated above thirty inches an hour, rather than matching whatever the original install used. A homeowner replacing turf that always drained a little slower than it should doesn't have to accept the same performance a second time; the new backing is chosen for what the yard needs now, not for consistency with a product that's being pulled out anyway.

Say you have a 2013-installed village front yard with rubber infill

Say you have a front lawn converted to turf in 2013 in one of Celebration's original villages, put in with a rubber crumb infill that was ordinary practice then, now matted near the walkway with a base that holds water after storms in a way it never used to. At roughly 13 years old the turf itself sits within a typical service life, but the infill doesn't belong on a plain lawn anymore under the state's rule, so a full replacement swaps it for silica sand or zeolite while the base gets rebuilt. Because the new lawn keeps the footprint CROA already approved, the Architectural Review Committee process for it tends to move faster than a first-time submittal would.

Sizing up the haul-off before the truck arrives

Old turf and infill from a full Celebration yard can add up to a substantial weight once it's rolled and stacked, and estimating that volume before the tear-out starts shapes how many trips a haul-off actually takes and how the crew stages material on site while work continues. Underestimating it mid-job means a delay waiting on a second trip, which is avoidable with a rough weight and volume estimate worked out from the yard's square footage before the first section of old turf ever comes up.

A base that looked fine and wasn't checked closely enough

Reusing a Celebration lawn's base without probing it in more than one spot risks missing a fines-crusted section that looks compacted and level but still isn't draining the way new, washed material would. That kind of shortcut doesn't show up as a problem on install day, since new turf goes down over it looking exactly as it should, but the same drainage failure the old lawn had can reappear within a season or two under turf that's otherwise brand new.

A like-for-like replacement clears CROA faster than a resized one

Because a full tear-out and relay counts as new construction under CROA's Design Guidelines, even a straightforward like-for-like replacement still goes to the Architectural Review Committee, unlike a small repair that stays inside an already-approved footprint. What changes is how quickly that submittal moves: reproducing the same shape, edge and lot line the earlier approval covered typically clears faster than a project that also grows the footprint toward the Front Façade Zone or the alley.

Rechecking capped valves once the season changes

An automatic sprinkler timer on a Celebration property sometimes still has a zone programmed for an area that no longer should run, even after the head itself was properly capped during replacement, and that zone activating against a capped line can build pressure against a fitting that was never meant to hold water indefinitely. Walking through the irrigation controller after a replacement and confirming every capped zone is also turned off at the timer closes a gap that a purely physical cap doesn't address on its own.

Questions people ask

How do I know if Celebration turf needs replacing instead of repairing?

It comes down to what a tear-out would find. Turf that's just matted on a base that still drains can often be repaired in place; a base that's crusted or holding water, or a rubber infill on a plain lawn, points toward a full replacement instead.

Does replacing older turf near a Celebration pond change the setback?

It can. An install that predates the state's current 10-foot setback gets brought in line with it during a full replacement, with a seawall or bulkhead as the one exception that keeps the edge where it already sits.

Does a like-for-like turf replacement still need CROA approval?

Yes, since a full tear-out and relay counts as new construction under the Design Guidelines. It typically clears the Architectural Review Committee faster than a first-time submittal, though, when the new lawn reproduces the shape and edge the earlier approval covered.
